newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian party to calls for end to strained ties.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian party to calls for end to strained ties.

text.p: One of Cambodia's two ruling political parties ended a four-day congress on Monday with calls to rebuild the strained ties with its coalition partner.

Chea Sim also told reporters his Cambodian People's Party boosted its central committee by 85 members to 153, renewed its commitment to holding elections by the end of 1998, and said the party favoured a proportional representation system.

"We continuously strive to consolidate the political alliance that dated back to before the (last) general election," the CPP leader said, refering to the 1991 and 1993 accords between the CPP and its coalition partner, the royalist FUNCINPEC party.
FUNCINPEC narrowly edged out the CPP in the last elections in 1993, but agreed to form a coalition government to avoid renewed fighting after more than a decade of civil war.

Ties between the two parties became strained last March when FUNCINPEC demanded a fairer share of power, and worsened further when both sides began wooing thousands of Khmer Rouge guerrillas who have defected to the government since August.
Chea Sim said the CPP wanted to end disputes peacefully.
"Political alliance requires that the concerned parties be sincere to each other and jointly preserve it. Only by so doing could that political alliance last," he said.

"Political competition in this multi-party and liberal democracy is a normal matter, but this competition must...not lead to confrontation which results in antagonistic and life-and-death issues," he added.
FUNCINPEC confirmed last week that it plans to form a new alliance with Khmer Rouge defectors and the opposition Khmer Nation Party.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, the FUNCINPEC leader, said the CPP was welcome to join the alliance, but CPP vice president and co-Premier Hun Sen turned him down.
Hun Sen said, however, that the CPP wanted to continue working with FUNCINPEC in government and parliament.
